criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural drinking water service delivery, infrastructure maintenance financing, and handpump functionality across rural municipalities and village communities in Mali.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines national decentralisation and water financing policy, municipal Sector Development Plans and Technical Units, and community water management institutions. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although Sections 3.1-3.2 and part of Section 3.4 discuss macro-governance background (aid dependency, decentralisation) and municipal planning/coordination (PDSECs and Sector Development Plans), Sections 3.3-3.6 directly analyse tariff and cost-recovery rules as well as local discretion/accommodation governing rural water service maintenance and availability: national user cost-recovery mandates, municipal-user O&M cost-sharing rules, informal case-by-case discretion on breakdown contributions accommodating community ability to pay, formal committee accounting required to access municipal repair co-funding, and village tariff rules (volumetric per-container or regular household tariffs adapted to seasonal women's savings groups and collective farming).
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative multi-level empirical case study drawing on collaborative fieldwork conducted with WaterAid and its partners in Mali in 2010 and 2011 (including dated interviews with municipal councillors and civil servants in November 2011, 2011 workshops with municipal officials and Technical Unit/NGO staff, analysis of 15 rural municipalities, 8 village case studies, and secondary DNH handpump functionality statistics). Note that Footnote 1 states that fuller data and results are reported in companion papers (Jones 2013a, b), making standalone empirical reporting relatively brief here, though primary qualitative fieldwork evidence is directly presented.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports rural drinking water service availability/reliability via municipal handpump functionality rates (90% functional in the municipality using a formalised local O&M cost-sharing rule and part-funding for repairs, compared with the 71% rural Mali average), alongside community O&M fundraising adequacy and ability-to-pay constraints relative to national full cost-recovery requirements.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and multi-level units of analysis (national policy, 15 WaterAid-supported rural municipalities including a focal Technical Unit municipality, and 8 case study villages in rural Mali), exposure (tariff, user cost-recovery, and municipal-community O&M cost-sharing rules and discretionary accommodations), outcome (handpump functionality/service reliability and O&M cost-recovery sufficiency), and study design (qualitative multi-level case study) are all identifiable, though quantitative sampling details are sparse because companion articles report fuller empirical data.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: The paper uses such an extended political economy analysis approach to understand the role of the international NGO WaterAid and its partners in Mali in relation to institutions for financing rural water services, drawing on collaborative research undertaken in 2010 and 2011.

This particular Technical Unit has adopted a specific approach to sharing the long-term costs of operation and maintenance between water users and the municipality by developing its own local interpretation of the ambiguous national policy (Jones 2013b).
The functionality rate of handpumps in this municipality at the time of research (90% functional) was significantly greater than the Mali average for rural areas of 71% (DNH 2010) (see Jones 2013b).

WaterAid’s other partners had not developed such clear specific procedures for determining the contribution of users in case of breakdowns. Instead, they used more informal discussions on a case-by-case basis. This lack of clarity over the exact division of responsibilities between users and other actors reflects both the ambiguity in national policy, and the responses of WaterAid’s partners to different levels of willingness and ability to pay amongst different communities (Jones 2013a).

A further part of the research on financing arrangements involved the identification by WaterAid’s partners of eight case study villages which were considered particularly successful at raising money for their contributions to the long-term costs of maintaining water infrastructure. Analysis of the case studies sought to understand whether their mechanisms for raising money were more successful because they employed the recommended national policies (paying per container collected or paying a regular tariff) or whether they were successful for other reasons.
Firstly, even communities identified as more successful in terms of fundraising rarely achieve the sums of money suggested as necessary by national policy.

raw_response.exposure: Rural water tariff and cost-recovery rules and local discretionary accommodations: national user cost-recovery policy, municipal Technical Unit O&M cost-sharing rules and repair co-funding vs informal case-by-case breakdown contribution negotiations, formal committee accounting requirements, and village-level bricolaged tariff structures (adapting household tariffs to seasonal women's savings groups and collective farming rather than rigid per-container or flat regular tariffs).
raw_response.outcome: Rural water point availability/reliability measured by municipal handpump functionality rate (90% functional in the focal municipality vs 71% rural Mali average) and community O&M revenue mobilisation adequacy relative to national cost-recovery requirements for sustaining water services.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural water sector in Mali (units of analysis: national policy level, 15 rural municipalities supported by WaterAid including municipal councillors/civil servants and municipal Technical Units, and 8 case study villages identified as relatively successful at water maintenance fundraising, studied in 2010-2011).
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative multi-level case study (2010-2011 fieldwork in Mali) satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2. Beyond its theoretical synthesis of political economy analysis and critical institutionalism, it empirically examines rule-type mechanisms directly governing sustained rural drinking water access—specifically national user cost-recovery rules, municipal-community O&M cost-sharing rules, case-by-case discretionary accommodation of user breakdown contributions based on community ability to pay, formal accounting requirements to access municipal co-funding, and locally adapted household water tariff schedules across 8 case study villages. It links local cost-sharing and repair co-funding to rural water service availability/reliability (90% handpump functionality in the focal municipality vs 71% across rural Mali) and documents affordability/revenue limits under national full cost-recovery rules. Confidence is set to medium because Footnote 1 notes that fuller empirical data and results from the same research are reported in companion articles (Jones 2013a, b), leaving methodological and village-level access outcome reporting relatively concise here.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative multi-level case study (collaborative fieldwork in 2010-2011 using interviews, stakeholder workshops, municipal institutional analysis, 8 village case studies, and secondary administrative handpump functionality data)
